Our reporting shows that co-Chief Executive Ted Sarandos had complained internally for months that Americans were spending less time watching Netflix and that the service was short on new hit shows.

Netflix is set to report third-quarter earnings after today’s closing bell and will try to answer Wall Street’s questions about its strategy.

   • Vice President JD Vance declined to back Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel’s coming elections, a break from Trump who has given the Israeli prime minister his backing.

   • Voters in Alberta chose to stay in Canada by a convincing margin, staving off an economic and political crisis for Prime Minister Mark Carney.

   • After more than half a century, New York brought a title to Madison Square Garden. Now, the Knicks and its owner are squabbling over new contracts.

READ IT HERE FIRST   Marine Le Pen is seizing on the chaos in France to present herself as leader in waiting.   The riots sweeping France have rocked the country’s political establishment, but while President Emmanuel Macron’s government struggles to maintain control, one person is positioned to emerge from the chaos with a strengthened hand : Marine Le Pen. The far-right leader has long cast France as a nation adrift, buffeted by waves of immigration and lawlessness that have torn at the country’s social fabric. As bands of rioters have descended on city centers across France, raiding city halls and looting thousands of stores, Le Pen has sought to present herself as the sole candidate in next spring’s presidential election willing to restore order. Le Pen’s approach has given her an air of inevitability in her pursuit of France’s highest office, reports Stacy Meichtry.

   5.   Nurses are in high demand—but they’re quitting in droves.   America’s nurses are more educated and better-paid than ever. Most have their bachelor’s degree. Their income has boomed since the pandemic to a median $97,550 a year, and their hands-on work isn’t easily automated away. Nursing schools have seen their ranks swell, minting thousands of new graduates every year. They’re also leaving the bedside in droves . Burnout and complaints about understaffing, verbal abuse and workplace violence are pushing many nurses off the front lines and into other careers where their skills are in high demand, reports Te-Ping Chen.

Netflix Won the Streaming Wars. Now It Faces Its Biggest Disruption in Years.
 
Plus, how the riots in France benefit Marine Le Pen, and why nurses are quitting in droves
 
 
A scene from the ‘East of Eden’ series on Netflix. GEOFFREY SHORT/NETFLIX/EVERETT COLLECTION
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

Netflix is writing a new script.

 

Last week, it abruptly replaced content chief Bela Bajaria just hours after a layoff of 1,000 employees that she helped engineer. By Monday, film chief Dan Lin was out too. The ousters signal that the streaming giant’s leaders feel the service needs a creative overhaul.

Our reporting shows that co-Chief Executive Ted Sarandos had complained internally for months that Americans were spending less time watching Netflix and that the service was short on new hit shows.

Netflix is set to report third-quarter earnings after today’s closing bell and will try to answer Wall Street’s questions about its strategy.

 

Ahead of that, we take you inside the streaming giant’s year of mounting troubles.

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

 
 
 

2. TODAY’S HEADLINES

 

• President Trump said he would be open to meeting with the leaders of Russia and China to discuss denuclearization.

 

• Vice President JD Vance declined to back Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel’s coming elections, a break from Trump who has given the Israeli prime minister his backing.

 

• Voters in Alberta chose to stay in Canada by a convincing margin, staving off an economic and political crisis for Prime Minister Mark Carney.

 

• After more than half a century, New York brought a title to Madison Square Garden. Now, the Knicks and its owner are squabbling over new contracts.

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

Marine Le Pen is seizing on the chaos in France to present herself as leader in waiting.

 

The riots sweeping France have rocked the country’s political establishment, but while President Emmanuel Macron’s government struggles to maintain control, one person is positioned to emerge from the chaos with a strengthened hand: Marine Le Pen. The far-right leader has long cast France as a nation adrift, buffeted by waves of immigration and lawlessness that have torn at the country’s social fabric. As bands of rioters have descended on city centers across France, raiding city halls and looting thousands of stores, Le Pen has sought to present herself as the sole candidate in next spring’s presidential election willing to restore order. Le Pen’s approach has given her an air of inevitability in her pursuit of France’s highest office, reports Stacy Meichtry.

 

5.

 

Nurses are in high demand—but they’re quitting in droves.

 

America’s nurses are more educated and better-paid than ever. Most have their bachelor’s degree. Their income has boomed since the pandemic to a median $97,550 a year, and their hands-on work isn’t easily automated away. Nursing schools have seen their ranks swell, minting thousands of new graduates every year. They’re also leaving the bedside in droves. Burnout and complaints about understaffing, verbal abuse and workplace violence are pushing many nurses off the front lines and into other careers where their skills are in high demand, reports Te-Ping Chen.

6. SEE THE STORY

 

We went to Greenwich to find out what the ultrarich want for the midterms.

 
 
Photo: John McColgan for WSJ
 

WSJ’s Annie Linskey: Greenwich, Conn., is a town that has been shorthand in political circles for one word: fundraising. Democratic and Republican donors throw open the doors of their beautiful homes and hold parties where candidates for office mingle, drink wine, munch on appetizers, and take questions from people they hope will fund their campaigns. It is also where I grew up. I went back to get a sense for what some of the town leaders—and donors—are thinking as we approach Donald Trump’s final midterms. I found that Democrats and Republicans here offered a similar refrain: Politics in the U.S. has got too extreme.

 
 
 

7. HAPPENING TODAY

 

• Trump is scheduled to hold a midterm rally in Greenville, N.C. 

 

• The legal battle between Dolly Parton’s estate and her nephew Bryan Seaver heads to court in Nashville, Tenn.

 

• The NBA regular season begins.

 

• Economic data: U.S. housing starts and building permits data are scheduled for release.

 

• Earnings: Netflix, General Motors, SpaceX, United Airlines, GE Aerospace, RTX

 

• 📰 Today’s paper

 
 
 

8. THE NUMBER

 
$1 billion
 

Real-estate giant CBRE is acquiring a company that equips data centers in a $1 billion deal, the latest sign that commercial real estate is tying its growth to the AI spending boom. CBRE has agreed to pay about $610 million in cash for London-based Onnec, plus up to $400 million tied to growth targets over several years. Onnec’s 800 employees install and maintain cabling and equipment racks inside data centers for major technology companies in Europe and Asia-Pacific.

 
 
 

9. AND FINALLY…

 

Step aboard for a nonstop day in the life of Carnival’s star cruise director.

 
 
JEFF LAUTENBERGER FOR WSJ
 

Carnival Cruise Line fans rework their itineraries to ensure they’ll be on her ship. Onboard, she can hardly walk a few feet without getting stopped for a hug or selfie. Several hundred thousand social-media followers track her comings and goings. You’ve probably never heard of Kyndall “Fire” Magyar. But for a certain segment of cruise enthusiasts, she’s about as big as it gets. As cruise director of the Carnival Jubilee, Magyar is the social engine of one of the world’s largest cruise ships. Her days can start at dawn and end after midnight.
